1:
Clarke opens on the title. Shophetim are not judges in the usual sense of men who decide controversies, but rulers with sovereign power who administer justice, make peace and war, and lead armies — the Carthaginian suffetes, the Athenian archons and the Roman dictators answering to them — yet neither hereditary nor popularly chosen, so that the government was a theocracy and the judges God's deputies. He calls the book's chronology extremely embarrassed, and dismisses the received way of reckoning the years of rest as a violent perversion of the ordinary meaning of terms; the author he takes to be one man writing later, most probably Samuel. Keil and Delitzsch set out the plan of the book: an introduction, the history of the several judges, and a twofold appendix.

The opening clause is the first difficulty, and Ellicott states it plainly. Most of what follows must have happened before Joshua died, since his death and burial are only reported afterwards, since the Israelites can hardly have sat still through a life of a hundred and ten years, and since the events reappear in the previous book almost verbatim. He runs through the escapes — narration by anticipation, supplied words, pluperfect verbs, a scribe writing Joshua for Moses — and rejects the last as unsupported by any manuscript or ancient commentator, preferring to think the sentence a general heading left standing when preface and appendix were added. Clarke never raises the question, and guesses only that the interval was short, the enemy taking their opportunity once their champion was dead. Henry's point is that Joshua left no successor in his own authority, so that the people had to consult the breastplate instead of a man.

Ellicott notes that the phrase used is not the usual one for asking the Lord but a rarer construction found again only later in this book, and takes it for consultation through the high priest by Urim and Thummim. On what those were he canvasses three theories — answers spelt out by a light playing over the twelve gems, the priest's mind abstracted by gazing on them, cut and uncut stones used like lots — before concluding that the truth was forgotten thousands of years ago and will never be recovered. Henry gives four reasons for Judah's precedence — most numerous, first in dignity and therefore first in duty, first served by the lot, and the tribe from which Christ should spring — with the rule that God appoints service according to the strength he has given. Ellicott adds that Judah camped eastward and always marched first, under a lion standard. On why Simeon is called Judah's brother, Gill and Ellicott appeal to their common mother; Keil and Delitzsch deny that is the reason and point instead to Simeon's lot lying inside Judah's. Ellicott, who gives both, adds that Simeon had fallen from fifty-nine thousand fighting men to twenty-two between the censuses.

Adoni-bezek is a title and not a name, Ellicott and Clarke agree, like Adoni-zedek. Both explain the mutilation alike, severed thumbs disabling a man from bow and sword and severed toes from flight; Ellicott adds that either would have cost him his throne, since no ancient people tolerated a maimed king, and grounds its fitness here in the law of retaliation. Clarke gathers the same custom from Aelian and Suetonius and derives our word poltroon from the Italian for a man without a thumb; but he doubts that seventy kings ever literally fed under a table, taking the phrase for a proverb of the meanest servitude. Henry reads it literally, and observes that the Israelites, who maimed him by the law of like for like, did not put him under the table, which would have savoured of a haughtiness unbecoming an Israelite. What both make the point is the confession: the spoiler is spoiled, and conscience speaks when God's judgments awaken it.
8:
Whether Jerusalem fell now or under Joshua is disputed from the first verse of the span. Gill reports the rabbis divided — some referring it back to Joshua's campaign, others urging that only Judah is named here where all Israel fought then — and offers the compromise that the city was taken twice, the Jebusites recovering it while Israel was busy elsewhere. Clarke reads the verse as a parenthesis about the earlier capture and supposes the same recovery, the Jebusites keeping their stronghold on Mount Zion until David. Ellicott is sharper: the English supplies the word had without warrant, as a gloss meant to push the conquest backwards, and the true account must be pieced out from the earlier book — the people slaughtered, the king beaten, the city burnt, and yet the Jebusites left holding either the citadel or the town, so that generations later a traveller could still refuse to lodge in what he called the city of a stranger.

Ellicott notes that going up is the idiom for a campaign and going down for a particular battle, as the Latin has it of descending into the line, the phrase arising from the habit of encamping on high ground wherever possible; and he sorts the three districts named — the hill country, the dry south, and the low maritime plain — assigning Hebron and Debir to the first, Zephath to the second, and the Philistine towns to the third. Clarke, Gill and Keil and Delitzsch all treat the section as a recapitulation of the previous book, Gill allowing as an alternative that there were two distinct expeditions. On Hebron Ellicott is full: midway between Jerusalem and Beersheba, once called Mamre after its chief and now the friend after Abraham, and named for Arba, whom some make the father of Anak and others the numeral four. The three names that follow he takes for clans of the Anakim, and disposes of the giant bones shown in Josephus's day as the remains of extinct animals mistaken for men.

Debir means the oracle, and its older name the city of the book, which Ellicott thinks may mark it as a seat of Canaanite learning. He raises a doubt about Caleb himself, whose descent from a grandson of Esau and whose name, if it means dog, he finds an unlikely one for a pure Israelite, so that a foreign origin has at least some probability. The relation between Caleb and Othniel he leaves open: the Hebrew will bear either that Othniel was Caleb's brother, marrying his niece at a great age, or that Kenaz was Caleb's brother and Achsah his cousin — the Masoretic pointing favouring the first. Henry, for his part, dwells on Caleb's delay in taking possession of Hebron, granted him a dozen years earlier but left unclaimed while he served the public, so content was he to be served last.

Achsah gets Ellicott's closest attention. Othniel was too modest to ask for himself and had refused her request, so she would not enter his house until she had carried her point; the field she asks for has the article, having become historical by the time this book was written; and the verb for lighting from her ass means not the usual gesture of reverence but a leap of eager impetuosity, though the old versions read it as a cry or a sigh, and Caleb's question is that of a father who cannot understand why his daughter will not go in to her bridegroom. In asking for the watered land at the foot of the slope she showed herself, Ellicott says, at once more provident and less bashful than her husband; the springs he glosses as bubblings, upper and lower, and reports the glen identified in his own century, green with an unbroken rivulet. Keil and Delitzsch note only that the word for spring stands here in a singular form.
16:
The Kenites bring a tangle of names. Ellicott holds Jethro and Reuel to be one man, the second being his priestly title in Midian, and makes him father of Zipporah and of Hobab, who alone consented to go with Israel as their caravan-guide; the Kenites themselves he takes for the elder branch of Midian, named from a chieftain Kain, living among the rocks by the gulf of Akabah and originally cave-dwellers. He notes that the text says the city of palm trees rather than Jericho, and suggests the name was avoided because it lay under a curse — a scruple nomads pitching their tents among its palms and balsams would not have shared. Clarke follows Calmet's account: the Kenites stayed with Israel through the wilderness, held a lot with Judah, lived in the palm city while Joshua lived, and moved south afterwards, whether from discontent with their portion or from pressure by the older inhabitants. Gill and Clarke both carry the family down to the Rechabites of Jeremiah's day.

Zephath, renamed Hormah, is a place of the ban. Keil and Delitzsch put it on the southern boundary and derive the name from the banning executed there, identifying the site with a ruin south of Elusa; Ellicott derives it from the same root and reads the conquest as the discharge of the vow Israel had made after being beaten back by the king of Arad; Clarke simply refers the whole transaction to that earlier episode.

The three Philistine cities produce the chapter's sharpest textual problem. Clarke sets out the Septuagint of the Vatican copy, which flatly negates the verse — Judah did not possess Gaza, nor Askelon, nor Ekron — notes that Augustine and Procopius read the same, that Josephus allows only two of the towns to have been taken, and that the whole subsequent history shows these cities in Philistine hands; if Judah took them, he says, they lost them again very soon. Ellicott reports the same negative and is more cautious, suggesting that the not may have been added conjecturally to remove a discrepancy, or may be a gloss upon took, and concluding only that the conquest was very transitory. Keil and Delitzsch read the order of the names as proof that the advance came from the south, and observe that by Samson's time all three were Philistine again.

The iron chariots draw Clarke's protest: were they too strong for Omnipotence? He holds the verse mistranslated, would end the previous sentence with the words about the Lord being with Judah, and follows the Chaldee paraphrast in supplying what the Hebrew leaves out — that it was afterwards, when they sinned, that the plain could not be cleared. Ellicott reaches the same sense from the grammar without moving anything, since the Hebrew avoids saying could not and says instead that there was no driving out: Judah was able, but its faith was cowed. He adds that the valley here means the broad kind between parallel hills and not the coastal plain, doubts on the evidence of the Nineveh sculptures and of Xenophon that scythed chariots existed so early, and clears away a patristic charge that the Kenites secretly helped the enemy, which rests on nothing but the Septuagint mistaking the word for chariot as the name Rechab. Gill records that the Targum reads the Word of the Lord for the Lord. Ellicott closes with a larger observation: after this chapter Judah nearly vanishes from the book, producing no judge and going unmentioned in Deborah's song, perhaps because the very security it had won left each tribe looking out for itself.
21:
The notice about Benjamin and the Jebusites says of Benjamin what the previous book said of Judah, and the commentators divide over the reason. Clarke concludes that the names must have been interchanged in one place or the other. Gill and Ellicott let the city straddle both lots — Gill citing rabbis who make Jerusalem not a walled town at all but a province, part Judah's, part Benjamin's and part still Jebusite, Ellicott assigning it properly to Benjamin and explaining its later attachment to Judah by David's capture of Zion, and adding that the Jebusites were tolerated there long afterwards under a prince of their own. Both Clarke and Ellicott draw the same inference from the phrase unto this day: since the writer speaks of the Jebusites as still in possession, the book must have been written before David's reign. Henry only remarks that Judah had set a good example which Benjamin failed to follow for want of resolution.

At Bethel the narrative moves from southern to central Palestine. Ellicott explains the town's importance by its place on the highway between Hebron and Shechem and by its associations with Abraham and Jacob, and notes that it is now a wretched village; he suspects, as with Jerusalem, that the tribal border may have separated the upper town from the lower. Henry supposes the line ran through it so that half belonged to each tribe, and that the vigour of the house of Joseph secured the whole. Clarke observes that Joshua had taken Ai but not Bethel, and reports that a good many manuscripts, with the Septuagint and the Arabic, read children of Joseph where the received text has house.

The man who showed the way divides the commentators sharply. Henry will not blame him if he acted from a conviction that the Lord was with Israel and the land was theirs by grant, any more than Rahab was to be blamed for sheltering the enemies of her country who were the friends of God; nor will he blame those who spared him, since one good turn requires another. Clarke is unsparing: however the thing is looked at, the man's conduct was execrable, a traitor's, buying his own life with the lives and property of his fellow citizens — and though the laws of war allowed Israel to use such a man and his information, that does not lessen the turpitude on his side. Ellicott, without moralising, notes that ancient armies were seldom able to storm a walled town and depended on blockade or betrayal, and compares the Persians taking Sardis by following a man who had climbed down after a fallen helmet. Keil and Delitzsch add that what he showed them was not the gate but a way in, and that the promise of favour meant the lives of himself and his household.

Where he went afterwards nobody knows. Keil and Delitzsch say the site of the new Luz is altogether unknown, and that the land of the Hittites cannot be fixed either, since Hittites appear at Hebron in Abraham's day, in the hill country later, and later still away to the north-east. Gill and Clarke both put it outside Canaan, Gill supposing either a flight before Joshua or an older colony settled abroad, Clarke guessing Arabia and taking the man himself for a Hittite. Ellicott inclines north, toward the Phoenician frontier, mentions a rabbinic tradition that the place was famous for purple dye, and observes that founding a new city under an old name was common enough — as Teucer, driven from Salamis, built another Salamis in Cyprus. Henry's comment is on the name itself: the man kept Luz, an almond tree, in preference to Bethel, which carried religion in it.
27:
The chapter closes with a descending roll-call, and Ellicott traces the historian moving up the country from the southern tribes. Manasseh left five towns unsubdued and in time only made their people serfs; Ephraim let Gezer alone, which Gill thinks was covered by a covenant made against God's express command; Zebulun took tribute from two towns Gill notes had been assigned to the Levites, which may explain the sloth and certainly aggravates it. Then the phrasing turns over: Asher is said to dwell among the Canaanites rather than the reverse, which Gill and Ellicott alike read as an admission that the older inhabitants were masters and the tribe there on sufferance — the climax of degradation, Ellicott calls it. Naphtali reduced two towns out of nineteen. Ellicott notes that Issachar is not mentioned at all, and suspects the contented subjection under which that tribe had bowed its shoulder to the yoke.

At the point where Israel grows strong enough to exact tribute instead of driving out, Ellicott stops for an excursus on the morality of the exterminating wars. Nations, he argues, must be judged by the standard of their own day and not by the advanced morality of later ages; the peoples of Canaan had sunk so low as to be practically irreclaimable, and to live among them would have been to learn their works, so that Israel believed extermination a duty and was moved to it by its better instincts. But he insists that the teaching of Christ has changed the world's moral conceptions altogether, and that no weight of evidence would now persuade us we were bidden to destroy a whole population; and he is severe on those who quote such commands to excuse later massacres, which he says is to obliterate the results of a long moral education. Keil and Delitzsch are concerned only with when the serfdom began, and argue against dating it as late as Solomon's reign.

The place-names are worked hard. Ellicott identifies Beth-shean as the town to whose wall the Philistines fastened Saul's body, later called Scythopolis in contempt of its inhabitants' barbarism, and standing in country the rabbis called the gate of Paradise; from Megiddo, he notes, comes the name Armageddon. Keil and Delitzsch follow Acco through its Greek and Ptolemaic names to the Acre of the crusaders, flourishing then and decayed since. On the mountain of Heres all agree the word means sun — Gill guessing either sun-worship there or the standing still of the sun at neighbouring Aijalon, while Ellicott and Clarke report that the Greek translators read the consonants differently, produced a mountain of potsherds, and rendered the two towns beside it as the place where the bears and the foxes are, Aijalon meaning gazelles and Shaalbim jackals.

Dan comes off worst of all. Ellicott calls the Amorites the highlanders of Palestine and the verb for what they did to Dan a squeezing; Keil and Delitzsch point out that Dan's allotment lay almost wholly in the plain, so that being pushed up into the hills excluded the tribe from its inheritance almost entirely and drove part of it to emigrate. Clarke reaches for modern parallels: the Britons driven into the mountains of Wales by the Romans, and the Indians pushed back into the woods by British settlers in America. Ellicott adds a sting to the relief that came, since the Amorites were made tributary not to Dan but to the Ephraimites who had rescued them, so that the help was at best somewhat selfish. The closing note on the Amorite border he takes either as explaining their stubbornness or as showing that only the southern frontier was ever secured; the rock named in it he and Keil and Delitzsch incline to read as Petra. Clarke ends by observing that few can be persuaded adversity is a blessing, though without it we should learn very little.
